solution:
The pink solution is a **stain**. In a fresh section only the cells that contain chloroplasts (such as mesophyll cells) look green; most other cells, like the epidermis, cortex, pith, xylem and sclerenchyma, have no chloroplasts and are colourless, so their outlines are hard to make out. When the section is immersed in the stain, the cells take up the colour, so the cell walls and the different tissues stand out clearly against each other. The epidermis, cortex, vascular bundles and pith can then be recognised easily under the microscope.
[Note: the chapter does not describe staining of sections, and does not name the stain or state which cell walls take it up.]

Scattered vascular bundles are the feature of a **monocot stem**, and in a monocot stem each vascular bundle is conjoint, collateral and **closed**, that is, without cambium. Increase in girth (secondary growth) needs a **vascular cambium**: in a dicot stem the intrafascicular cambium and the interfascicular cambium join to form a complete **cambial ring**, which is possible only because the bundles lie in one plane, in a ring. In a monocot stem there is no cambium in the bundles and the bundles are scattered, so no cambial ring can form. However many bundles there are, the stem therefore cannot grow in girth; secondary growth is absent.

It is a **concentric vascular bundle**, in which one vascular tissue completely encircles the other. If the **xylem is encircled by phloem**, it is a **hadrocentric** bundle; if the **phloem is encircled by xylem**, it is a **leptocentric** bundle. The book describes concentric vascular bundles as always closed, since no cambium lies between the two tissues.

The wood formed by the vascular cambium depends on the season. During the **favourable season** the cambium is very active and forms **spring wood (early wood)**: broad xylem bands, lighter in colour, tracheids with thin walls and wide lumen, few fibres and low density. During the **unfavourable season** it forms **autumn wood (late wood)**: narrow xylem bands, darker in colour, thick walls with narrow lumen, abundant fibres and high density. A light band of spring wood next to a dark band of autumn wood shows up as a distinct ring in a cut log, one for each favourable and unfavourable season. The log with rings came from a tree that grew where the seasons alternate; in the other log the cambium worked at much the same rate all the time, so the wood formed is uniform and no rings are seen.
[Note: the chapter does not use the term growth ring or annual ring, and does not describe the wood of a tree growing without seasonal change.]

Distinct rings form only where there is a sharp difference between a **favourable** and an **unfavourable season**. In the favourable season the cambium forms light, broad, low-density **spring wood**, and in the unfavourable season it forms dark, narrow, high-density **autumn wood**; the contrast between the two bands each year makes a clear ring. A place with a marked unfavourable season, like Kashmir, gives this sharp contrast, so its trees show distinct rings. Where conditions stay much the same through the year, the spring and autumn wood differ little, so the rings are faint or not seen.
[Note: the chapter does not discuss the climate of Kashmir or Maharashtra; the comparison of their seasons is assumed from the question.]

Scattered bundles alone do not prove a monocot stem; the **type of vascular bundle** decides it. In a **monocot stem** each bundle is **conjoint, collateral and closed**: xylem and phloem lie on the same radius with xylem inside and phloem outside, the xylem is endarch with a **lysigenous (protoxylem) cavity**, and each bundle is surrounded by a **sclerenchymatous bundle sheath**. On observing again, the student saw that each bundle of the rachis was **concentric**, with one tissue completely encircling the other (xylem in the centre surrounded by phloem, the **hadrocentric** type), not collateral. So he agreed that it was not a monocot stem.
[Note: the chapter does not state that the fern rachis has concentric (hadrocentric) vascular bundles; it only defines the concentric types.]

A stopper of this kind is made of **cork (phellem)**, the tissue cut off on the outer side by the **cork cambium (phellogen)**. The walls of cork cells are **suberized**, so cork is **impervious** and does not allow water to enter. Because water cannot soak into it, the stopper does not decay even after many years. Durable wood such as **heartwood** resists decay in a similar way, as its elements are filled with oils, gums, resins and tannins (extractives) that make it resistant to pathogens.
[Note: the chapter does not mention stoppers or explain rotting; it states only that cork is impervious and that heartwood is resistant to pathogens.]

The section was of a **monocot (isobilateral) leaf**. In such a leaf both surfaces are equally illuminated, since both can face the sun, and the two surfaces show similar structure and are equally green. A monocot leaf bears **stomata on both surfaces** (it is **amphistomatic**). In a dicot (dorsiventral) leaf, stomata are generally absent from the upper epidermis and are many on the lower epidermis, which is why the student expected them only on one side. So stomata on the upper surface do not mean the slide was upside down.

- A **stoma** is a small gateway (pore) in the epidermis.
- Each stoma is guarded by two specially modified cells called **guard cells**: **kidney shaped** in dicots and **dumbbell shaped** in monocots.
- The guard cell has an **inner thick wall** facing the pore, a nucleus and a few **chloroplasts** that carry out photosynthesis.
- The guard cells are surrounded by **subsidiary cells**, and beyond them lie the ordinary epidermal cells.
- The stoma, guard cells and subsidiary cells together form the **stomatal apparatus**.
- Guard cells change their **turgor pressure**, which opens and closes the stoma; stomata therefore play a vital role in the **exchange of gases and water vapour**.
- Below each stoma lies an air space, the **sub-stomatal chamber**, through which the mesophyll is in contact with the atmosphere.
- In a dicot leaf stomata are mostly on the lower epidermis; a monocot leaf bears them on both surfaces.
[Note: the textbook says the guard cells are "collectively called as Stomata"; stomata is the plural of stoma, the pore with its guard cells.]

- Growth in length by the apical meristem is **primary growth**; increase in **girth** of root and stem is **secondary growth**. It is seen in dicotyledonous plants and gymnosperms and is brought about by the **lateral meristems**.
- In the dicot stem the **intrafascicular cambium** (between primary xylem and primary phloem) becomes active, and the medullary ray cells next to it become meristematic again (**dedifferentiation**) to form **interfascicular cambium**. The two join into a complete **cambial ring**.
- The cambium cuts off cells on both sides: those towards the pith become **secondary xylem** and those towards the periphery become **secondary phloem**; secondary xylem is generally more than secondary phloem.
- Spring (early) wood forms in the favourable season and autumn (late) wood in the unfavourable season. The inner, durable heartwood is non-functional, while the outer sapwood conducts sap.
- When the epidermis ruptures, outer cortical cells form the **cork cambium (phellogen)**, which cuts off **cork (phellem)** outside and **secondary cortex (phelloderm)** inside; the three together form the **periderm**. **Lenticels** in the bark allow exchange of gases and water vapour.
- In dicot and gymnosperm roots, conjunctive parenchyma becomes meristematic and adds secondary xylem and phloem in the same way.
- Monocot stems lack cambium, so secondary growth does not take place, except as **anomalous secondary growth** by accessory cambium in *Dracaena*, *Agave*, palms and the root of sweet potato.
[Note: the textbook says the increase in diameter is due to the vascular cambium "present in the outer cortical layer"; it is the cork cambium that arises from the outer cortex, while the vascular cambium lies between xylem and phloem.]

- Sclerenchyma cells are living when produced but **dead at maturity**, so they lack cytoplasm, and their walls are very **thick**.
- The thickening is due to the **uniform deposition of lignin** (lignified walls), unlike collenchyma, whose cellulose walls are thickened unevenly with cellulose and pectin at the corners, and parenchyma, whose cellulose walls are thin.
- Because the wall is so thick, the cell cavity (**lumen**) is narrow.
- The walls carry **pits** that keep the cells interconnected: in **fibres** the pits are narrow, unbranched and oblique; in **sclereids** they are deep, branched and straight.
- Such walls make sclerenchyma a **mechanical tissue**: fibres give mechanical strength and sclereids give stiffness.
- Commercial fibres such as jute, flax and hemp come from sclerenchyma fibres.

| Point | Monocot (stem) vascular bundle | Dicot (stem) vascular bundle |
|---|---|---|
| Type | Conjoint, collateral and **closed** | Conjoint, collateral and **open** |
| Cambium and secondary growth | Cambium absent, so no secondary growth | A strip of cambium between xylem and phloem, so secondary growth takes place |
| Arrangement | Numerous and **scattered** in ground tissue | Arranged in a **ring** |
| Bundle sheath | Each bundle surrounded by a **sclerenchymatous bundle sheath** | No such sheath; pericycle above the bundles is sclerenchymatous (hard bast) in sunflower |
| Xylem | Endarch, with a **lysigenous (protoxylem) cavity**; vessels rounded | Endarch, no such cavity; vessels angular |

| Point | Xylem | Phloem |
|---|---|---|
| Material conducted | **Water and minerals** | **Organic food** from source (generally the leaf) to sink (other plant parts) |
| Conducting elements | **Tracheids and vessels** (hadrome) | **Sieve tubes** (sieve cells in pteridophytes and gymnosperms), helped by **companion cells** (leptome) |
| Living or dead | A dead tissue; only xylem parenchyma is living | A living tissue; only phloem fibres are dead |
| Lateral conduction and storage | Xylem parenchyma carries out lateral (radial) conduction of water and stores starch and tannins | Phloem parenchyma carries out lateral conduction of food and stores food, latex, resins and mucilage |
| Mechanical role | Gives mechanical strength to the plant body (lignified tracheids, vessels and xylem fibres) | Phloem fibres give mechanical support |

| Point | Dicot leaf | Monocot leaf |
|---|---|---|
| Type of leaf | **Dorsiventral**: horizontal, upper surface faces the sun and is darker than the lower | **Isobilateral**: both surfaces equally illuminated and equally green |
| Mesophyll | Differentiated into **palisade** (closely packed elongated cells) and **spongy** parenchyma (loose cells with intercellular spaces) | **Not differentiated** into palisade and spongy tissue |
| Stomata | Generally absent on the upper epidermis, many on the lower epidermis | Present on **both** surfaces (amphistomatic) |
| Guard cells | Kidney shaped | Dumbbell shaped |
| Veins and vascular bundles | Closed bundles of varying size, each with a parenchymatous bundle sheath, xylem towards upper and phloem towards lower epidermis | **Parallel veins**; bundles conjoint, collateral and closed |

The diagram is a transverse section of a dicot (dorsiventral) leaf, as in the book's Fig. 8.17 (T. S. of dicot leaf). Its labels are:

- Adaxial (upper) epidermis
- Palisade mesophyll
- Spongy mesophyll
- Air cavity
- Sub-stomatal cavity
- Stoma
- Abaxial (lower) epidermis
- Bundle sheath
- Xylem
- Phloem

The upper epidermis carries a cuticle, the palisade and spongy mesophyll carry out photosynthesis, and the stomata of the lower epidermis connect the spongy mesophyll with the atmosphere.

The diagram is a transverse section of a monocot root, as in the book's Fig. 8.15. Its labels are:

- Root hair
- Epiblema
- Cortex
- Endodermis
- Pericycle
- Protoxylem
- Metaxylem
- Phloem
- Pith

The diagram should show more than six xylem bundles alternating with phloem (the **polyarch** condition) and a large, well-developed pith.

The diagram is a transverse section of a dicot (sunflower) stem, as in the book's Fig. 8.16, drawn as a diagrammatic outline and a part enlarged. Its labels are:

- Hair (trichome)
- Cuticle
- Epidermis
- Hypodermis (collenchyma)
- General cortex (parenchyma)
- Endodermis
- Starch grains
- Resin duct
- Hard bast
- Phloem
- Cambium
- Metaxylem
- Protoxylem
- Wood parenchyma
- Medullary rays

The vascular bundles are conjoint, collateral and open, arranged in a ring, with endarch xylem and a pith of large parenchymatous cells in the centre.

**Diagram 1: a stoma in surface view (dicot type, kidney-shaped guard cells)**

- **Guard cell** (top pointer): a specially modified epidermal cell; two of them guard the stoma. They have a few chloroplasts for photosynthesis, and their change in turgor pressure opens and closes the stoma.
- **Inner thick wall** (second pointer): the thick wall of each guard cell that faces the stomatal pore.
- **Nucleus** (bracketed pointers): the nuclei of the two guard cells.

The stoma allows exchange of gases and water vapour; it is surrounded by the epidermal cells.

**Diagram 2: location of meristems in a shoot (Fig. 8.2)**

- **Apical meristem** (shaded tip): terminal in the shoot; forms the growing point and increases the **length** of the plant body.
- **Intercalary meristem** (shaded bands, bracketed): present at the top or base of a node; mainly active in monocots and short lived.
- **Lateral meristem** (vertical strips): along the sides of the central axis; increases the **girth** of stem and root, e.g. intrafascicular cambium in gymnosperms and dicots.

**Diagram 3: a root tip**

- **Apical meristem** (lower pointer, shaded tip): the growing point of the root; in the root it is **subterminal**, lying behind the root cap, and it increases the length of the root.
- **Mature region of the root** (upper pointer): the part above the tip, made of permanent tissue whose cells have lost the capacity to divide; root hairs arise from the epidermis here and absorb sap from the soil.

The upper pointer of diagram 3 has no label in the book's Fig. 8.2, so it is read here as the mature part of the root behind the growing tip.
[Note: the chapter does not name the zones of the root tip; Fig. 8.2 labels only the apical meristem in the root.]

Diagram a is the **T. S. of a dicot root** (as Fig. 8.14): it has an exodermis below the epiblema and four separate xylem groups alternating with four phloem groups, with almost no pith.

Labels, from the top: **epiblema** with root hairs (pointer to the pale outer layer), **exodermis** (dark layer), **cortex**, **phloem** (dark patch), **protoxylem** (small cells at the outer end of a xylem arm), **metaxylem** (large central xylem cells). The ring of **endodermis** and the **pericycle** inside it complete the labelling.

| Part | Characteristics |
|---|---|
| Epiblema | Outermost single layer without cuticle; some cells prolonged into unicellular root hairs |
| Exodermis | After the death of epiblema, the outer layer of cortex becomes cutinized |
| Cortex | Several layers of parenchymatous cells that store food and water |
| Endodermis | Innermost layer of cortex; barrel-shaped cells whose radial walls bear **Casparian strips** of suberin; passage cells near protoxylem |
| Pericycle | Single parenchymatous layer below the endodermis, bounding the stele |
| Vascular bundles | 2 to 6 **radial** bundles (diarch to hexarch); xylem **exarch**; conjunctive tissue between xylem and phloem |
| Pith | Narrow, parenchymatous |
| Secondary growth | Takes place later by a cambium ring between xylem and phloem |

The top-left pointer ends on the pale outer layer at the base of a root hair, so it is read as the epiblema bearing root hairs.

Diagram b shows **parenchyma containing chloroplasts (chlorenchyma)**: loosely arranged, rounded, thin-walled living cells full of chloroplasts, with spaces between them, as in the mesophyll of a leaf.

Labels: **cell wall** (top-left pointer), **vacuole** (top-centre pointer, the clear central area), **chloroplast** (bottom-centre pointer, the dark green bodies), **intercellular space** (bottom-right pointer, the gap between cells).

| Feature | Characteristics |
|---|---|
| Cells | Living, isodiametric, round to oval |
| Cell wall | Thin, made of cellulose |
| Contents | Cytoplasm with a prominent nucleus, a large vacuole and many chloroplasts |
| Arrangement | Distinct intercellular spaces |
| Function | Photosynthesis; also gaseous exchange and storage |
| Occurrence | Mesophyll of leaves, as part of the ground tissue |

The top-left pointer ends at the edge of the outermost cell, so it is read as the cell wall rather than the chloroplasts inside.
[Note: the chapter does not describe chlorenchyma as a separate tissue; it states that parenchyma performs photosynthesis and that leaf mesophyll contains chloroplasts.]

Diagram c is a **stoma (stomatal apparatus) in surface view**, as in Fig. 8.11 (epidermal cells), with kidney-shaped guard cells.

Labels: **epidermal cells** (the two pointers on the left), **subsidiary cell** (top right), **inner thick wall**, **nucleus**, **stomatal pore**, **guard cell** (lowest pointer).

| Part | Characteristics |
|---|---|
| Epidermal cells | Compactly arranged without intercellular spaces; central large vacuole, thin cytoplasm and a nucleus |
| Subsidiary cells | Surround the guard cells; part of the stomatal apparatus |
| Guard cells | Two kidney-shaped cells (dicot type) with a few chloroplasts; change in turgor pressure opens and closes the stoma |
| Inner thick wall | The thick wall of the guard cell facing the pore |
| Nucleus | One in each guard cell |
| Stomatal pore | Small gateway for exchange of gases and water vapour |

Diagram d is the **T. S. of a dicot (dorsiventral) leaf**, as in Fig. 8.17.

Labels: on the upper left, **bundle sheath**, **xylem** and **phloem**; on the right from top to bottom, **adaxial (upper) epidermis**, **palisade mesophyll**, **air cavity**, **spongy mesophyll**, **sub-stomatal cavity**, **abaxial (lower) epidermis**; at the bottom, **stoma**.

| Part | Characteristics |
|---|---|
| Upper epidermis | Single layer of tightly packed, barrel-shaped cells without chloroplasts; distinct cuticle; stomata generally absent |
| Palisade mesophyll | Below the upper epidermis; closely packed elongated cells with abundant chloroplasts |
| Spongy mesophyll | Loosely arranged, irregular cells with chloroplasts and intercellular spaces (air cavities) |
| Vascular bundles | Closed, of varying size, each with a parenchymatous bundle sheath; xylem towards upper, phloem towards lower epidermis; no cambium |
| Lower epidermis | Single layer with thin cuticle and many stomata |
| Sub-stomatal cavity | Air space at each stoma |

| Characters | Dicot leaf | Monocot leaf |
|---|---|---|
| Stomata | Generally absent on the upper epidermis, many on the lower epidermis; guard cells kidney shaped | On both surfaces (amphistomatic); guard cells dumbbell shaped |
| Intercellular space | Palisade cells closely packed; spongy cells loose with large intercellular spaces (air cavities) | Mesophyll cells closely packed with few, small spaces (as Fig. 8.18 shows) |
| Venation | not stated in the chapter | Parallel veins |
| Vascular bundle | Closed, of varying size, each with a parenchymatous bundle sheath; xylem towards upper, phloem towards lower epidermis | Conjoint, collateral and closed |
| Mesophyll cells | Differentiated into palisade and spongy parenchyma | Not differentiated into palisade and spongy tissue |

[Note: the chapter does not state the venation of the dicot leaf; it gives parallel veins only for the monocot leaf. The monocot spacing is read from Fig. 8.18, as the text does not describe it.]
